label: Single-line nuclei, in vivo (23Na, 17O, 7Li, 35Cl, 39K)
reference: Each of these nuclei is referenced to its own aqueous standard, and in every case the in vivo line sits on that zero: 23Na to an NaCl solution or gel phantom, 35Cl to the chloride of the same NaCl solution, 39K to a KCl solution, 7Li to aqueous LiCl (1 M in practice; IUPAC uses 9.7 M LiCl in D2O), and 17O to liquid water. So the ppm axis here is a formality rather than a working scale: nothing in these experiments is identified by its position.
note: For 23Na, 17O, 7Li, 35Cl and 39K the in vivo experiment returns a single resonance rather than a spectrum, and it is the free ion itself for 23Na, 35Cl, 39K and therapeutic 7Li, and H2 17O water for 17O; alkali and halide shifts barely move with the ionic environment, so each line sits at 0 ppm on its own reference and the measurement reports a concentration, not a position. In particular the intracellular and extracellular 23Na pools are NOT separated by any chemical shift, and are told apart only by their different relaxation behaviour (biexponential T2*, triple-quantum filtering) or by an added paramagnetic shift reagent, which is an animal-only trick.

peaks.name: 23Na
peaks.full: Sodium-23: tissue Na+, intracellular and extracellular unresolved
peaks.note: One line from all NMR-visible tissue sodium, about 40 mM in brain, referenced to an aqueous NaCl phantom at 0 ppm. Intracellular sodium (10 to 15 mM) and extracellular sodium (140 to 150 mM) differ in frequency by far less than the in vivo linewidth, so they are one peak: the split seen in animal work is imposed by a shift reagent, not by tissue, with Dy(PPP)2 (7-) moving the extracellular line 10 to 20 ppm upfield of the intracellular one. In ordered tissue such as cartilage or tendon the line can carry a residual quadrupolar splitting, which is a fixed splitting in hertz, not a chemical shift. Heights in this panel rank roughly how much in vivo signal each nucleus gives and are heavily compressed; each stem is the entire spectrum of its own nucleus.

peaks.name: 17O
peaks.note: The only thing in vivo 17O sees is water, and it is also the reference at 0 ppm. The 1H-17O J-coupled triplet collapses to one broad singlet through fast proton exchange and fast quadrupolar relaxation (spin 5/2). Natural abundance is about 0.038 percent, roughly 20 mM of H2 17O in tissue water, which serves as the internal concentration reference; a CMRO2 study simply watches that same line grow as inhaled 17O2 is metabolised to H2 17O. Neither 17O2 gas nor hemoglobin-bound 17O2 is MR visible, which is why only the metabolic product appears and no second peak ever does.

peaks.name: 7Li
peaks.full: Lithium-7: Li+ in tissue during lithium therapy
peaks.note: Li+ in patients on lithium, a few tenths of a millimolar in brain (well below the serum level), as a single line against aqueous LiCl at 0 ppm. Alkali metal shifts are nearly blind to the ionic environment, so intracellular and extracellular lithium fall on the same frequency exactly as sodium does; compartments are inferred from biexponential T2, about 15 ms intracellular against about 300 ms extracellular in rat brain at 7T, never from position. T1 in the human head is long, about 4.6 s, which sets the repetition time rather than any spectral consideration.

peaks.name: 35Cl
peaks.note: Tissue chloride, the counter-ion to sodium and overwhelmingly extracellular (about 100 to 110 mM in plasma against a few millimolar inside cells), as one line at 0 ppm against the same aqueous NaCl reference used for 23Na. 35Cl is spin 3/2 with a large quadrupole moment and only about 0.5 percent of the per-nucleus sensitivity of 1H, so human work is confined to 7T and above and reports a concentration map. Chloride bound to protein relaxes too fast to be detected at all, so what is measured is NMR-visible chloride rather than total chloride.

peaks.name: 39K
peaks.full: Potassium-39: tissue K+, almost entirely intracellular
peaks.note: Tissue potassium, roughly 100 mM in muscle and nearly all of it inside cells, as a single line at 0 ppm against an aqueous KCl phantom. It has the worst sensitivity of any nucleus here, about 0.05 percent of 1H per nucleus, so a human scan at 7T takes around 30 minutes for one number per voxel. In ordered muscle the line is not quite a singlet: residual quadrupolar coupling adds satellites about 200 Hz out when the calf lies parallel to B0, and because that is a splitting fixed in hertz it corresponds to roughly 14 ppm at 7T and to more ppm at lower field, so it is deliberately not drawn on this ppm axis.
